package_info.why_malicious: The UNIZA ransomware is a malicious Windows binary that encrypts user files in key directories and demands a ransom for decryption. It disrupts access to user data, employs psychological manipulation by simulating remote typing of the ransom note in the Command Prompt, and attempts to extort victims by demanding payment via Bitcoin. The malware does not drop ransom note files, instead displaying the ransom message live in the console, making detection and recovery more difficult.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, immediately after execution of the ransomware binary
execution_context.file_location: malware main executable (Portable Executable file, Windows binary)
required_permissions: read/write access to user profile directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
for each file in %userprofile% and Desktop:
    encrypt(file)
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudo-code (actual implementation likely in C/C++ or similar compiled language)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates all files and directories under %userprofile% and Desktop, applies an internal encryption routine to each file, overwrites the original files with the encrypted versions, and renders user data inaccessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated, bulk encryption of user files in profile directories is a core ransomware tactic and is never performed by legitimate software without explicit user consent and backup.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not encrypt all user files in-place without user knowledge or consent. This destructive behavior is designed to extort victims and is fundamentally at odds with normal software operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or archiving tools may access and copy many files, but do not encrypt them in-place or overwrite originals without clear user approval and recovery options.
key_indicators: Automated enumeration and modification of large numbers of files in %userprofile% and Desktop
In-place encryption and overwriting of user data
No user interaction or consent requested before destructive action
Absence of backup or recovery mechanisms

execution_context.trigger: After file encryption completes, during the same runtime session
execution_context.file_location: malware main executable (Portable Executable file, Windows binary)

malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudo-code (actual implementation likely in C/C++ or similar compiled language)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After completing file encryption, the code launches the Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe), programmatically simulates keystrokes to type out the ransom note character by character in the console window, and instructs the victim to pay a ransom via Bitcoin, creating the illusion of remote attacker presence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Simulating keystrokes to display a ransom note in the Command Prompt is a psychological manipulation tactic unique to ransomware, not used by legitimate software for user notification.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not simulate remote typing in the console to display messages, especially not ransom demands. Legitimate notifications use standard dialogs or files, not simulated keystrokes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some installer scripts may open a console window for user prompts, but do not simulate keystrokes to type messages or demand ransom.
key_indicators: Programmatic launching of cmd.exe from a non-interactive process
Simulated keystroke injection to the console window
Display of a ransom demand message via live typing
No ransom note file dropped to disk

attack_chain.action: Malware is executed on the victim's Windows system, typically delivered via phishing email or malicious attachment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initiation of file system enumeration and encryption

attack_chain.action: Enumerates all files and directories under %userprofile% and Desktop, encrypts each file in place using an internal encryption routine.
attack_chain.leads_to: User data becomes inaccessible due to encryption

attack_chain.action: Launches Command Prompt (cmd.exe) and simulates keystrokes to display the ransom note, demanding payment via Bitcoin and providing contact instructions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is psychologically pressured and instructed to pay ransom for decryption

behavioral_signatures: Automated, bulk file access and modification (encryption) in %userprofile% and Desktop directories within a short time frame
Launching cmd.exe from a non-interactive process and simulating keystrokes to display a ransom note
Absence of dropped ransom note files; ransom message is only shown via live console output
file_indicators: No new file extensions appended to encrypted files (original filenames retained)
No ransom note file dropped to disk; ransom note is only displayed in the Command Prompt

SHA256 hashes of known UNIZA ransomware samples: eefa1271d1a2a937d0baa3f0c7d904941151d6c8f915aed4dd51f10fa5d09b2a, d9a3f2ad7cfc6989cc4da117d5a4f8097362aad6b91391e89746d68d8d7aa29f, 9092ef0beeef1b147c13da3f3259f4a075f3bfb2414c39f9108395435ac9887c
network_indicators: No direct command-and-control (C2) or data exfiltration observed; ransom note instructs victim to contact via TikTok and pay via Bitcoin
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for processes that rapidly access and modify large numbers of files in %userprofile% and Desktop directories, especially if followed by launching cmd.exe and simulating keystrokes to display a ransom note. Alert if no ransom note file is dropped but a ransom message appears in the console. Use known file hashes to block or quarantine UNIZA ransomware samples. Flag unusual process behaviors such as simulated typing in the Command Prompt, which is not typical for legitimate applications.
